name: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT)
lead: Dihydrotestosterone (DHT, 5alpha-dihydrotestosterone, androstanolone) is an endogenous androgen made from testosterone by the enzyme 5alpha-reductase, mainly in tissues such as the prostate, skin and hair follicles. It binds the androgen receptor more strongly than testosterone and cannot be converted to estrogen by aromatase [1][29]. It drives development of the male external genitalia in the fetus and, at puberty, facial and body hair, sebum production and prostate growth, and it is implicated in male-pattern hair loss and prostate enlargement [1][2][3][29]. Its role in looks is therefore two-sided: it helps produce beard growth and a masculinised appearance, and it is the androgen behind scalp-hair miniaturisation in people with a genetic predisposition.

In looksmaxxing communities, DHT is discussed in two ways: as something to lower, through 5alpha-reductase inhibitors such as finasteride and dutasteride for hair loss, and as something to apply, in homemade or compounded topical DHT gels that some users say can enhance facial bone masculinisation during puberty, beard growth or penile size [4][5]. A prescription DHT gel was studied in a phase 2 trial in older men with low testosterone, and topical DHT has been used clinically in boys with micropenis [6][7]. No published trial has tested topical DHT for facial structure in people without an endocrine disorder.

paras: DHT circulates at roughly 5 to 10 percent of the level of testosterone and is formed mainly at the site of action [1]. In male fetuses, high local DHT concentrations are needed to form the penis, scrotum and prostate; a sterile review of micropenis notes that conversion of testosterone to DHT and its action at the androgen receptor are necessary for normal penile development [6]. At puberty, DHT promotes facial and body hair, sebum production and voice deepening; in genetically susceptible adults it shortens the growth phase of scalp hair follicles, leading to miniaturisation [1][2][8]. Reviews describe different follicles responding in opposite ways: beard follicles are stimulated and scalp follicles in androgenetic alopecia are suppressed [8][2]. A classic 1974 study of 5alpha-reductase deficiency in men described an inherited form of pseudohermaphroditism due to impaired DHT formation [9].

Wikipedia gives the figures that about 5 to 7 percent of testosterone is converted to DHT, roughly 200 to 300 micrograms per day, mostly in peripheral tissues such as skin and liver, and that circulating DHT is about one-tenth of total testosterone. Most DHT acts locally in the tissues where it is made, and it is broken down to weaker androgens such as 3alpha-androstanediol [29].

Hair follicles respond differently by site. Pattern hair loss is described as driven by DHT acting on dermal papilla cells of scalp follicles, which miniaturise in genetically susceptible people, while beard and body follicles are stimulated by the same androgen [31][8]. In 1942 James Hamilton reported that male pattern baldness does not occur in castrated men unless they receive testosterone, an observation that pointed to androgens as necessary for the condition [31]. Roughly 80 percent of balding men have bald fathers, indicating a strong inherited component [31].

The clearest natural evidence about DHT comes from 5alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency, a rare autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in the SRD5A2 gene. People with a 46,XY karyotype are born with a range of atypical genital development, from female-appearing to undervirilised male genitalia [32]. A 1961 description of the condition was followed by the 1974 confirmation of its cause in studies of 24 people in the Dominican Republic and two in Dallas, Texas [32][9].

At puberty, rising testosterone produces virilisation in affected people, including increased muscle mass, voice deepening, pubic hair and a growth spurt, with normal bone density; facial and body hair stay reduced, male-pattern baldness does not occur and the prostate is underdeveloped [32]. These observations are the basis for the description of DHT as important for genital, prostate, beard and scalp-hair biology but not required for muscle, voice or height changes at puberty [32][29].

Adolf Butenandt's group first synthesised DHT in 1935 and it was confirmed as an endogenous hormone in 1956, according to Wikipedia [29]. The 1974 characterisation of 5alpha-reductase deficiency showed that affected people had small prostates and little baldness, and Merck developed finasteride (MK-906) as an enzyme inhibitor after those reports; it was patented in 1984 [9][33].

The US FDA approved finasteride for benign prostatic hyperplasia in 1992 as Proscar (5 mg) and for male pattern hair loss in 1997 as Propecia (1 mg) [33][30]. Dutasteride, which blocks all three enzyme isoforms, followed for prostate enlargement in 2001 and was approved for hair loss in South Korea in 2009 and Japan in 2015 [30]. DHT gel in forum culture is a separate development: threads promoting it as a puberty tool appear on looksmax.org alongside discussion of 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors [4][5].

Finasteride blocks the type 2 and 3 enzymes and lowers circulating DHT by roughly 65 to 70 percent at the prostate dose, while dutasteride lowers it by about 95 percent [30][33]. In the 1998 trial of men with male pattern hair loss, finasteride improved hair counts [12], and a trial comparing dutasteride with placebo and finasteride examined the stronger inhibitor [13]. Wikipedia reports two meta-analyses finding about 15 percent hair regrowth with finasteride, and that dutasteride is more effective than finasteride for scalp hair [33]. Topical finasteride spray has also been tested [14]. Wikipedia's article on pattern hair loss notes that finasteride tends to work better at the crown than at the front [31].

Clascoterone, a topical androgen-receptor inhibitor, is approved for acne [16]. Because lowering DHT can reduce beard-follicle stimulation as well as scalp-hair loss, communities discussing both goals sometimes weigh the two [31][8].

Reported effects of 5-ARIs include sexual dysfunction in roughly 3.4 to 15.8 percent of users in studies, breast tenderness and gynecomastia in about 1.3 to 1.5 percent [30][33]. A 2010 Cochrane review found sexual side effects more common than placebo in the first year and no longer distinguishable after two to four years, though some men report persistent symptoms after stopping, and post-finasteride syndrome is described in a 2019 BMJ editorial as ill defined and controversial [33]. The European Medicines Agency confirmed in 2025 that suicidal thoughts can occur with finasteride, mainly at the 1 mg dose [33]. The FDA warns that 5-ARIs lower PSA and may be linked to high-grade prostate cancer, and Merck settled lawsuits over persistent side effects in 2018 [33][30].

DHT gel has been tested for treating symptoms of low testosterone in men aged 55 to 80 (phase 2, 128 participants) [7] and an earlier-stage study measured its effects on prostate tissue in healthy men [10]. Hormonal therapy for micropenis may include intramuscular or topical testosterone or topical DHT [6]. Imaging with a fluorinated DHT analogue has been tested in prostate cancer [11].

Because DHT mediates androgenetic alopecia, finasteride and dutasteride, which block 5alpha-reductase, are used for hair loss. Systematic reviews and randomized trials report efficacy for these and for topical finasteride [2][12][13][14][15]. Clascoterone, a topical androgen receptor inhibitor competing with DHT, is approved for acne [16].

A registered phase 2 study in 128 men aged 55 to 80 tested DHT gel for symptoms of late-onset hypogonadism [7]. A phase 1/2 study of 31 healthy men examined DHT effects on prostate tissue [10]. No study has tested topical DHT for facial bone growth, beard growth or penile size in healthy people, and none has examined it in adolescents with typical development. A rugby-player trial and a 12-week randomized trial examined whether creatine changes DHT; these concern creatine, not DHT use [17][18].

A looksmax.org poster who cites a study reports that two years of DHT gel was associated with an 84 percent fall in testosterone alongside a roughly sevenfold rise in DHT, and that users on the forum take this as evidence that the gel suppresses the natural axis [19].

Reported effects of exogenous androgens as a class include suppression of the body's own testosterone production, acne and mood changes. Forum members report emotional effects and, as noted above, suppression with DHT gel [19][20]. A key theoretical concern in adolescents is that androgens advance bone maturation and can shorten final height, although users in the community argue that DHT, not aromatizable, avoids estrogen effects; no study has examined this [4]. Because DHT promotes prostate growth, 5alpha-reductase inhibitors are used in prostate enlargement, and the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial of finasteride examined prostate cancer rates [21]. Grokipedia states that elevated DHT has not been linked to higher prostate cancer risk in most studies [1].

Threads on looksmax.org have promoted DHT gel as a "pubertymaxing" tool, arguing that DHT is the main driver of brow ridge, jaw, cheekbone and voice development, is two to three times more androgenic than testosterone and does not aromatize, and that applying it during puberty could enhance masculine bone structure [4]. The author noted the topic is "often mocked" on the forum [4]. Other threads ask whether it works for penile length or girth, mandible growth, or after puberty, with reports of both claimed growth and doubt that the gel works for penile growth [5][19][22][23][24][25]. Some users pair it with topical finasteride for hair, which commenters question [5]. On T Nation, DHT mainly appears in lab panels for men on testosterone therapy, with high DHT linked by users to acne and libido questions [26][27].

timeline.event: Hamilton reports that male pattern baldness does not occur in castrates unless testosterone is given [31].
DHT confirmed as an endogenous hormone [29].
5alpha-reductase deficiency confirmed in people in the Dominican Republic and Dallas, linking DHT to male genital development [9][32].
Merck patents finasteride, developed after the 5alpha-reductase deficiency reports [33].
Finasteride approved for benign prostatic hyperplasia (Proscar) [33][28].
Finasteride approved for male pattern hair loss (Propecia) [33].
Finasteride trial in men with androgenetic alopecia published [12].
Phase 2 trial of DHT gel in older men with low testosterone begins [7].
Merck settles lawsuits over persistent sexual side effects of finasteride [33].
European Medicines Agency confirms suicidal thoughts can occur with finasteride [33].

lore.intro: Topical DHT gel is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, in guides, success claims and skeptical threads about face, beard, penis and puberty [4][19][22][23]. Discussion of DHT-lowering drugs for hair appears alongside it, as many users weigh hair against facial masculinity [5].

claims.claim: DHT gel during puberty enhances facial bone masculinity
claims.believers: A forum guide says DHT is the key driver of brow, jaw and cheekbone development and recommends applying it during the pubertal window [4].
claims.experts: No published study has tested topical DHT for facial bone development in people without an endocrine disorder; reviews describe DHT's role in puberty and fetal development [1][6].

claims.believers: Posters report claimed growth in length and girth from using the gel, citing micropenis literature [19][24].
claims.experts: Clinical use of topical DHT is described for micropenis, a defined disorder; no studies were found in people without the condition [6].

claims.believers: A poster citing a 24-month study notes an 84 percent testosterone decrease with a sevenfold DHT rise, and others agree it is suppressive [19].
claims.experts: The DHT gel trial in older men with low testosterone measured symptoms and hormones; its results are not available [7].

claims.claim: Some users report DHT gel does not work for penile growth
claims.believers: A thread title and replies argue the gel does not work for penile size in people without a disorder [22].
claims.experts: No controlled study addresses this in typical men.

claims.claim: Lowering DHT with finasteride or dutasteride protects hair
claims.believers: Users compare finasteride and dutasteride and say dutasteride is stronger [5].
claims.experts: Trials report that finasteride and dutasteride improve hair counts in androgenetic alopecia, and systematic reviews rank oral options as effective [2][12][13][15].

claims.claim: Low DHT means weaker facial masculinity and beard growth.
claims.believers: Users who discuss finasteride warn that lowering DHT could reduce beard or facial development, while DHT gel advocates say more DHT builds a stronger face [4][5].
claims.experts: People with 5alpha-reductase type 2 deficiency have reduced facial and body hair but virilise otherwise at puberty [32]; no trial has tested DHT levels against facial bone structure in typical people.

claims.claim: Post-finasteride side effects can persist after stopping.
claims.believers: Some forum users and patients report lasting sexual or mood symptoms after stopping finasteride.
claims.experts: A Cochrane review found sexual side effects equal to placebo after two to four years, while a 2017 review found 1.4 percent with lasting erectile dysfunction, and a BMJ editorial called post-finasteride syndrome ill defined and controversial [33].

card.summary: The potent androgen behind puberty and balding; DHT gel is a forum favourite for face and penis claims with no trials in healthy people.
card.note: Topical DHT gel is not an approved US product; hormone suppression reported by users.

quick.overview:
DHT is a hormone made from testosterone that shapes male genital development and puberty changes, and it is also the hormone behind male-pattern baldness. Forum users apply DHT gel hoping for a more masculine face, beard or penis size.

DHT gel has been studied in older men with low testosterone and used in boys with micropenis, but no trial has tested it for looks in people without a hormonal disorder.
quick.mechanism: DHT binds the androgen receptor more strongly than testosterone does and cannot turn into estrogen. Applied as a gel, it is absorbed through the skin and raises DHT in the blood.
quick.risks: Users and a forum-cited study describe suppression of the body's own testosterone with DHT gel. Androgens can cause acne and mood changes, and their effect on adolescent growth is unstudied. DHT gel is not an approved US product.
